title: Trump refuses to disclose transition donor names
description_short: Trump refuses to disclose transition donor names
description_medium: As of March 3, 2025, the Trump-Vance transition had not disclosed its donors. Unlike earlier transitions, it had not signed a General Services Administration memorandum that would require disclosure or agreed to the same contribution limits. The GSA said the team was not required to release donor names because it declined the services and funds covered by that agreement. The arrangement left the transition’s private financing opaque, but the linked report does not establish a legal violation.
description_long: Six weeks into the second Trump term, the Trump-Vance transition had not made public the names of people and organizations that funded its planning, according to the linked account. Previous transitions had agreed to disclose donors within 30 days and limit contributions, but the Trump-Vance team did not sign the General Services Administration memorandum that offered those terms. A GSA spokesperson said the team was not required to disclose transition donations because it did not accept the services and funds covered by the memorandum. The transition operated largely with private funding, and Trump-Vance Transition Inc. was registered in Florida as a nonprofit that did not have to disclose donors to the IRS. The account says the rules barred using the funds to enrich transition officers but allowed payments for services or support for political candidates. It also reports that the transition team declined to say whether it would adopt the earlier $5,000 contribution cap. The lack of disclosure made the transition’s donor base difficult to assess, but the source does not establish that the team violated a legal disclosure requirement or that donors received policy favors. The event is a choice of a private funding arrangement and non-disclosure, not a proven illegal payment scheme.

title: Trump threatens to deport Tesla protesters
description_short: Trump threatens to deport Tesla protesters
description_medium: In a Truth Social post in March 2025, Trump said Tesla protesters should be sent to an El Salvador prison he called a “slave prison,” and described its conditions sarcastically as “lovely.” The statement followed protests against Elon Musk and his role in the administration. It was a threat, not a report that protesters were arrested or deported; the linked account identifies no deportation order against them.
description_long: Donald Trump used a Truth Social post in March 2025 to say Tesla protesters should be sent to a prison in El Salvador, calling it a “slave prison” and describing the facilities as having “lovely conditions.” The comments came during protests against Tesla and Elon Musk, whose Department of Government Efficiency work had prompted demonstrations. The linked account placed the statement after Trump’s administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act in a separate immigration action and a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order against that action. It also referred to a Justice Department warning of severe punishment for some protesters, but those developments do not show that Tesla demonstrators were actually transferred abroad. The account documents Trump’s public threat and rhetoric about El Salvador’s prisons; it does not identify a named protester, an immigration case, a deportation order or a completed removal arising from the post. The threat should be distinguished from an implemented policy. The source provides no evidence that the government acted on the suggestion or that the protesters were eligible for deportation under any cited authority.

title: Trump: ICE deports 3 U.S. citizen children to Honduras
description_short: Trump: ICE deports 3 U.S. citizen children to Honduras
description_medium: In April 2025, immigration authorities removed three U.S.-citizen children from Louisiana to Honduras with their mothers in two separate cases. The children were four, seven and two years old. ICE said the second mother chose to take her two-year-old; she said she was not given a choice. A federal judge criticized the process as lacking “meaningful process.”
description_long: The linked account reports that three U.S.-citizen children from Louisiana were sent to Honduras with their mothers in two removals on consecutive days, April 24 and 25, 2025. In the first family, the mother had a deportation order and her daughters, ages four and seven, were citizens; the younger child was reported to have cancer. In the second family, the mother and older daughter had removal orders, while the two-year-old was a U.S. citizen. ICE said the second mother chose to have the toddler accompany her. The mother later said she had not been given a choice and was instructed what to do. A federal district judge criticized the process for lacking “meaningful process,” and family members were pursuing legal action. Attorneys questioned how the families’ options and communication were handled. The source does not establish that the children themselves had removal orders; their legal situations differed from their mothers’. It documents the removals and the competing accounts about parental choice, alongside the judge’s criticism. The available material does not resolve the families’ later legal status or the outcome of any proceedings, so those consequences should not be inferred.

title: Trump: RFK Jr. fires all CDC vaccine panel members
description_short: Trump: RFK Jr. fires all CDC vaccine panel members
description_medium: On June 9, 2025, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. The committee was scheduled to meet later that month, and HHS said the meeting would proceed. The linked account says Kennedy had promised Senator Bill Cassidy during confirmation not to alter the panel; the source does not establish the full process for selecting replacements.
description_long: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 members of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices on June 9, 2025. The committee was due to meet as early as June 25, and HHS said the meeting would continue as planned even though replacement members had not yet been announced. The linked account notes that 13 of the 17 members had been appointed the previous year and that committee members ordinarily serve four-year terms. It also reports that Kennedy had told Senator Bill Cassidy during confirmation hearings that he would not alter the panel. Kennedy later argued that members had conflicts related to pharmaceutical funding; the account says committee rules screen members for conflicts and require recusal where appropriate. The source links the removal to uncertainty around COVID-19 vaccine recommendations for pregnant women, but the materials do not establish that the panel dismissal caused a specific change in access or insurance coverage. The documented event is the removal of the full committee and the stated plan to continue its scheduled meeting. The membership, rationale and subsequent recommendations are separate questions that require later records.

title: Trump: California farms claim 70% of workers are gone
description_short: Trump: California farms claim 70% of workers are gone
description_medium: California farm owners, supervisors and workers interviewed by Reuters estimated that 70% of the state’s farm labor had been detained, deported or had disappeared during immigration raids. The linked account describes missed shifts and crops at risk of spoiling, but the figure comes from interviewees rather than a statewide workforce survey. Reuters also cited California’s large share of U.S. fruit, nut and vegetable production.
description_long: Reuters reported on June 30, 2025, that California farm owners, supervisors and workers said immigration raids had sharply reduced the available workforce during peak harvest. Interviewees estimated that 70% of the state’s farm labor had been detained, deported or had disappeared. The figure was an estimate from people Reuters interviewed, not a statewide survey or administrative count. One farmworker, who had spent decades in U.S. fields, said many colleagues had stopped coming to work because they feared being separated from their families. Farmers told Reuters that crops were going unpicked and produce was at risk of rotting, with some operators worried about closing. The article noted California produces more than a third of the country’s vegetables and more than three-quarters of its fruits and nuts, with nearly $60 billion in agricultural sales in 2023. Those figures describe the importance of the state’s sector, not measured losses caused by the raids. The reporting records the concerns and estimates of interviewees but does not quantify statewide labor losses, crop damage or resulting price increases. The 70% figure should remain attributed to those sources rather than presented as a confirmed statewide total.

title: Trump threatens to end critics' citizenship
description_short: Trump threatens to end critics' citizenship
description_medium: On July 12, 2025, Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that he was giving “serious consideration” to taking away comedian Rosie O’Donnell’s citizenship. He called her a threat to the country and humanity. The post documents a public threat against a named critic; the supplied material reports no legal proceeding or government action to revoke her citizenship.
description_long: On July 12, 2025, Donald Trump used Truth Social to say he was giving “serious consideration” to taking away Rosie O’Donnell’s citizenship. The post described the comedian as a threat to the country and to humanity. It was a public statement directed at a prominent critic, not a signed order or an agency action. The supplied account does not report a citizenship review, a court case or any other government process involving O’Donnell. It also does not identify a legal basis for the threatened action or document a later step to implement it. The distinction matters because a statement about considering an action does not establish that the government has taken it. The record supports describing Trump’s words and their target; it does not establish that O’Donnell’s citizenship was changed or that a formal procedure began. The post is therefore a documented threat, while any claim about its legal effect or practical consequences would require separate evidence.

title: Trump visits the White House roof
description_short: Trump visits the White House roof
description_medium: On August 5, 2025, Trump visited the White House roof with architect James McCrery and described a proposed ballroom expansion as a $200 million project. He told reporters he was taking a walk and said he would pay for the work while also referring to contributions. The linked account includes no approved budget, donor list or construction decision.
description_long: Donald Trump went onto the White House roof on August 5, 2025, with architect James McCrery, whom the linked account identified as overseeing a proposed ballroom addition. Trump told reporters he was “taking a little walk” to look at future projects and described the proposed expansion as costing $200 million. When asked about financing, he said he would pay for it and also referred to contributions. The account documents a site visit and the president’s public description of a proposed project. It does not provide a formal budget, donor commitments, a financing agreement, construction approval or a historic-preservation review. Trump’s remarks therefore do not establish that the project had been fully funded or cleared to proceed. The visit brought a proposed change to the White House into public view, but the supplied facts do not describe the design, construction schedule or later outcome. The event can be recorded as a presidential site visit and project announcement while leaving its funding and approval status unresolved.

title: directs Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to use all available funds to
description_short: President Trump directs Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to use all available funds to pay the US military during the shutdown in a Truth Social post
description_medium: During the October 2025 federal shutdown, Trump said he had directed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to use available funds to pay service members on October 15. The Office of Management and Budget told Congress it intended to use Defense Department research-and-development funds, and a spokesperson said two years of such funds were available. The post announced a plan; it did not establish that paychecks had been issued.
description_long: On October 11, 2025, during a federal shutdown that had lasted 10 days, President Donald Trump posted that he was directing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to use available funds to pay U.S. military personnel on October 15. Trump blamed Democrats for the funding lapse and said the administration had identified money for the payments. NBC News reported that the Office of Management and Budget notified Congress of its intent to use Department of Defense research-and-development funds; an OMB spokesperson said two years of those funds were available. The announcement came after Senate votes failed to reach the threshold needed to advance a temporary funding measure. The post was an announced plan to cover military pay during the shutdown, not evidence that the money had already been transferred or that all affected personnel received pay on the promised date. The available report does not establish the legal authority ultimately used, the amount drawn from research accounts or the final payment outcome. Those details are separate from Trump’s public directive and the administration’s stated funding approach.

title: Trump suggests invoking Insurrection Act
description_medium: On October 6, 2025, Trump said he would invoke the Insurrection Act if necessary, one day after a judge blocked a separate plan to deploy federal troops in Portland. He said he might act if people were being killed or courts, governors or mayors were holding the administration up. The statement floated possible military involvement in civilian law enforcement; no invocation or deployment under the Act is documented.
description_long: On October 6, 2025, Donald Trump publicly said he would invoke the Insurrection Act “if it was necessary.” The remark came one day after a federal judge blocked a separate plan to deploy federal troops in Portland, Oregon. Trump said he would act if people were being killed or if courts, governors or mayors were holding the administration up, adding that he wanted cities to be safe. The Insurrection Act provides a route for a president to use the military in domestic law enforcement under specified conditions; the linked account says it had not been used since the 1992 Los Angeles unrest. Trump’s statement was conditional and did not itself invoke the law or direct troops to Portland. The source reports no order, deployment under the Act or resulting law-enforcement operation. The event is a public suggestion of using a rarely invoked authority in the context of a court-blocked deployment plan. Any account of the legal basis or operational consequences would require a later order or court record, neither of which is identified here.
